the Stony Creek granitic rocks of southern New England are probably 616 ± 79 m.y. old and that they were emplaced at a high structural level during the Alleghanian orogeny.
the Stony Creek pluton was formed during Avalonian orogen and remobilized during the Taconian orogeny.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the origin and tectonic history of the Stony Cree granite, which is a large, relatively homogeneous, massive to migmatized granite body that crops out in central Connecticut.
the geology and geochemistry of the Stony Brook dome, the most southern of a chain of domes that extends along the Bronson Hill antichlinorium in Connecticut and Massachusetts.
the geologic evolution of the Bronson Hill anti-clinorum in southern Connecticut and eastern Massachusetts.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Stony Creek and Oliverian granites were formed in the same general region and time, and both have been extensively remobilized and deformed since their original crystallization, but that the two granites have different isotopic and geochemical characteristics.
the Rb/Sr systematics of the Stony Brook granite indicate that it was remobilized, and that the remobilized granite was emplaced at a time of high heat flow and high strain rates.
the Stony Creek and other similar granitoids are not necessarily the result of anorogenic, post-orogenic, or even anatexis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Rb/Sr isochron method is not always reliable for determining the age of granitic plutons, especially if they have undergone significant remobilization and metamorphism.
the Stony Creek pluton was emplaced during a Paleozoic orogenic event, probably in the Late Devonian or Early Mississippian (Taconian), and then remobilized during the Acadian orogeny.
